abstract.p: Graphene-like materials are renowned for their excellent electrical conductivity, large surface area, and high energy storage capability. In this study, three-dimensional (3D) interconnected graphene-like porous materials were synthesized from Sesbania, a sustainable biomass, via acid-assisted hydrothermal carbonization, followed by KOH activation. The resulting material (SE_GLC) features interconnected open pores within graphene-like sheets and boasts a surface area of 1140 m2/g. Its performance as an electrode in a symmetric supercapacitor was evaluated using a cost-effective 12 m NaNO3 “water-in-salt” (WIS) electrolyte to enhance energy density by widening the voltage range. The SE_GLC//SE_GLC pouch cell achieved a stable operating voltage of 1.9 V, delivering a high gravimetric energy density of 23.83 Wh/kg and a power density of 189.83 W/kg. Notably, even at a specific power of 5.69 kW/kg, it retained a specific energy of 9.49 Wh/kg. This work highlights the successful synthesis of interconnected graphene-like materials from biomass and their exceptional electrochemical performance with an economical WIS electrolyte, underscoring their potential for sustainable energy storage solutions.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p:
Supercapacitors have gained recognition as advanced energy storage devices due to their high power density, fast charging/discharging capabilities, safety, and extended cycle life. −
Among these, electrochemical double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) stand out for their ability to store energy by forming double layers of ions on the electrode interphase. They exhibit a superior rate capability and cycling stability compared to pseudocapacitor-based supercapacitors. However, their practical application is limited by their inherently low energy density, posing challenges in meeting the escalating long-term energy demands of the electric vehicle industry and grid energy storage systems. −
Addressing this critical challenge requires improving the energy density of EDLC-based supercapacitors through the development of advanced electrode materials and/or the selection of electrolytes with wide operating voltage ranges.

Two-dimensional carbonaceous nanostructures, especially graphene-based materials, are emerging as promising electrode candidates for EDLC-based supercapacitors. Their large surface area facilitates charge storage, while their two-dimensional nature shortens ion transport pathways, ensuring high electrical conductivity. However, graphene tends to restack due to the π–π interactions between graphene sheets during electrode preparation. This restacking reduces the accessible surface area for ion diffusion, resulting in a lower specific capacitance than theoretical values. ,−
To address this issue, graphene-like porous materials have garnered significant interest. These materials feature a framework structure constructed from graphene-like layers, , offering excellent electrical conductivity and high porosity. These properties promote rapid ion and electrolyte transport, contributing to high rate capability. , Additionally, their well-defined network structure prevents the restacking of graphene nanosheets, , collectively enhancing their electrochemical capacitive performance. Nevertheless, previous studies have often relied on complex and costly processes for synthesizing graphene-like materials. −
Consequently, there is growing interest in developing environmentally friendly, cost-effective, and straightforward synthesis methods using renewable resources for graphene-like carbon production. Biomass has emerged as an attractive precursor for graphene-like carbon due to its renewable nature, sustainability, and affordability. Typically, graphene-like materials can be obtained from plants by pyrolyzing their ultrathin lamellar structures, which are composed of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. Previous research has demonstrated the successful production of graphene-like materials from various biomass sources, which have been utilized as electrode materials in supercapacitors. These sources include flower petals, hemp, walnut shells, coconut shells, spruce bark, hazelnut shells, and orange peels. Thus, there is a significant opportunity to explore new biomass sources that are widely available and otherwise considered waste, to prepare graphene-like porous materials for use as electrode materials in supercapacitors. Notably, the choice of biomass precursor plays a crucial role in determining not only the structural properties of the resulting carbon but also the economic feasibility and scalability of the synthesis process. Sesbania was introduced in this work as a sustainable and underutilized precursor for preparing graphene-like carbon. Sesbania is a fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing plant commonly found in rice fields and wetlands across Thailand. Although it is occasionally used for soil improvement and animal feed, it is often considered an unwanted species. Its soft, fibrous structure makes it particularly well-suited for carbonization, offering a promising route to convert waste biomass into high-value graphene-like materials for energy storage applications.

While organic electrolytes can widen the voltage window of supercapacitors (often exceeding 3 V), they have notable disadvantages, including toxicity, low thermal stability, and flammability. Consequently, aqueous electrolytes have been explored as safer and more stable alternatives. However, the operating voltage of aqueous electrolytes is limited to approximately 1.23 V due to water decomposition via hydrogen evolution reactions (HER) and oxygen evolution reactions (OER), which restricts their practical use. , To overcome these challenges, superconcentrated water-in-salt (WIS) electrolytes-where dissolved salts greatly outnumber water molecules-have been introduced. This innovation enables an increased operating voltage for electrochemical energy storage devices, potentially reaching a voltage window of up to 3 V. −
In WIS electrolytes, most water molecules participate in ion solvation shells, leaving minimal free water molecules to undergo water-splitting reactions. Additionally, the formation of a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer, similar to those found in nonaqueous electrolytes, can suppress HER, further enhancing the electrochemical stability window. ,, Despite their superior electrochemical performance compared to traditional dilute aqueous electrolytes, WIS electrolytes have drawbacks such as low conductivity, high viscosity, , and relatively high cost, which hinder their commercial viability. To address these limitations, sodium nitrate (NaNO3) has emerged as a low-cost, environmentally benign alternative that offers lower viscosity and higher conductivity than other highly concentrated salts. ,, With a concentration of up to 12 mol/kg (molality), sodium nitrate solutions can effectively serve as WIS electrolytes. These advantages make NaNO3 a practical and cost-effective candidate, particularly for aqueous supercapacitors.

Despite extensive research on biomass-derived carbons and WIS electrolytes, ,,,, their combined use, particularly the integration of graphene-like carbon into cost-effective WIS systems and the impact of varying salt concentrations on electrochemical performance, remains underexplored. This study fills this gap by combining Sesbania-derived graphene-like carbon (SE_GLC) with a 12 m NaNO3-based WIS electrolyte, while also investigating the effect of NaNO3 electrolyte concentration on the graphene-like carbon. A three-dimensional (3D) interconnected graphene-like material was synthesized from Sesbania via acid-assisted hydrothermal carbonization (HTC), followed by chemical activation. The resulting SE_GLC was utilized as the electrode material in a symmetric pouch cell. The SE_GLC//SE_GLC device operated stably at 1.9 V, delivering an energy density of 23.83 Wh/kg and a power density of 189.83 W/kg. These findings confirm the electrochemical viability of both the Sesbania-derived graphene-like material and the NaNO3 WIS electrolyte. This integrated, low-cost, and scalable strategy offers a sustainable route for next-generation aqueous supercapacitor systems (Scheme ).

caption.title: Representation of the Synthesis of Sesbania Graphene-like Carbon (SE_GLC) and Its Application as an Electrode in a Symmetric Water-in-Salt Based Supercapacitor

sec.title: Materials and Chemicals
sec.p: Sesbania was obtained from a rice field in Ubon Ratchathani, Thailand. All chemicals and solvents were of analytical grade and were used directly without additional purification. Ethyl alcohol (C2H5OH, 99.9%), hydrochloric acid (HCl, 37%), nitric acid (HNO3, 69.0%), and potassium hydroxide (KOH, 85%) were provided by Reagents, Duksan, Merck, J.T.Baker, and LobaChemie, respectively. The electrodes were prepared using super P (99.9%) from Alfa Aesar and 1-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, 99.5%) from QReC. Poly­(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) was acquired from Sigma-Aldrich. Sodium nitrate (NaNO3, 99.0%), utilized as the electrolyte, was purchased from KemAus.

sec.title: Sesbania Pretreatment
sec.p: The pretreatment was carried out to remove undesired contaminants. Sesbania was first cut into small pieces and soaked in 1 M HNO3 for an hour. The chopped Sesbania was then rinsed with deionized (DI) water until the pH reached approximately 7. It was subsequently dried for 4 h at 105 °C in an oven (Memlert Germany, UN30). Finally, the dried Sesbania was ground into a powder for an hour at 350 rpm using a FRITSCH Planetary Ball Mill.

sec.title: Hydrothermal Carbonization
sec.p: A 0.5 M HNO3 solution (100 mL) was added to the as-prepared Sesbania powder (10 g), which was then placed in a Teflon-lined container in a stainless-steel autoclave. The autoclave was heated in an oven at 220 °C for 8 h. The resulting solid product was obtained by filtering and repeatedly washing it with ethanol and DI water. The final product was dried at 105 °C for 4 h and labeled as SE_HTC.

sec.title: KOH Activation
sec.p: The SE_HTC and KOH were mixed at a weight ratio of 1:1 (SE_HTC (g): KOH (g)). The mixture was heated under a nitrogen atmosphere at 800 °C for 1 h (Carbolite, Stf 16/450, 5 °C/min heating rate). The resulting sample was rinsed with 1 M HCl and DI water until the pH was neutral. Finally, the material was dried at 105 °C for 4 h and labeled as SE_GLC.

sec.title: Material Characterization
sec.p: The morphology of the sample was studied using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, JEOL, JSM-7610F Plus) in conjunction with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDX, Oxford Instrument). The structure of the synthesized materials was analyzed using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Bruker) and Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.54056 Å). Nitrogen adsorption–desorption isotherms were measured at 77 K using a Micromeritics, MicroActive for ASAP2460 instrument. The specific surface area and the pore size distribution of the samples were determined using the Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) and Barrett–Joyner–Halenda (BJH) methods. Raman spectra were obtained with a Raman spectrometer (SENTERRA II, 532 nm). Wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS) measurements were carried out at beamline 1.3 W of the Synchrotron Light Research Institute (SLRI), Thailand. The carbon sample was placed on an aluminum frame with Kapton windows. Synchrotron X-ray (9 keV) radiation was applied, and the WAXS data were recorded with SX165-CCD detectors. The sample-to-detector distance (SDD) was 140 mm, providing a 2θ Cu range of 10–46°. The exposure time was 300 s. Silver behenate and 4-bromobenzoic acid were used as calibration standards. The WAXS data were radially integrated using the SAXSIT program developed by SLRI staff to obtain 1D scattering data. Background subtraction was performed using a measurement of Kapton tape. The WAXS data were also used to determine the components and structure of the prepared carbon materials. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed using a PHI Versaprobe 4 Scanning XPS system equipped with a monochromated Al Kα X-ray source to evaluate the surface functional groups and chemical composition of the materials. Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectra were recorded using a PerkinElmer Spectrum 3 FTIR spectrometer over the wavelength range of 4000–500 cm–1.

sec.title: Electrode Preparation
sec.p: The materials were mixed with super P and PVDF at a weight ratio of 8:1:1, followed by the addition of NMP as the solvent to create a slurry. The slurry was subjected to sonication for 30 min (GT SONIC, D6, 40 kHz). It was then coated onto a graphite paper substrate (100 μm thick) and dried overnight at 105 °C. The active material loading was around 2 mg/cm2.

sec.title: Three-Electrode Electrochemical Evaluation
sec.p: All electrochemical tests were performed using a Metrohm Autolab (PGSTAT302N) in a three-electrode setup at room temperature. The as-prepared electrode served as the working electrode, an Ag/AgCl electrode was used as the reference electrode, and a Pt wire functioned as the counter electrode. The electrolytes used were 1m, 3m, 7m, and 12m NaNO3 solutions, where m denotes the concentration in molality (molsalt/kgwater), with water as the solvent.

The ionic conductivity and viscosity of the electrolytes were measured using a conductivity meter (Mettler Toledo, Greifensee, Switzerland) and a Ubbelohde viscometer (ISO/TR 3666, 0.17%), respectively. Cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) were applied to evaluate the electrochemical performance of the samples. CV tests were conducted at scan rates ranging from 10 to 100 mV/s. The specific capacitance (C s, F/g) was determined using the following formula 1 Cs=(∫Idv)(v)(m)(ΔV) Where v is the scan rate (V/s), C s is the specific capacitance, ∫Idv is the half area of the corresponding CV curve, ΔV is the potential window (V) and m is the mass of the material (g).

The specific capacitance in the three-electrode system was also calculated from GCD measurements using the following equation 2 Cs=(I)(Δt)m(ΔV) Where Δt is the discharging time (s), m is the total mass of material (g), I is the applied current (A), and ΔV is the potential window (V). The EIS tests were also assessed over a frequency range of 0.01 Hz to 100 kHz, with an applied voltage of 0 V and an amplitude of 10 mV.

sec.title: The Pouch Cell Preparation and Full Cell Electrochemical Evaluation
sec.p: The slurry was prepared by mixing the active material, Super P, and PVDF in NMP at a weight ratio of 8:1:1. After sonication for 30 min, the slurry was coated onto graphite paper with an active material loading of approximately 3 mg/cm2 and a coating thickness of around 150 μm. The coated electrodes were then dried overnight at 105 °C. The pouch cell was prepared using electrolytes, glass microfiber filters (Whatman GF/C), stainless steel sheets, plastic bags, and coated graphite paper (a diameter of 1 cm). The glass microfiber filters were soaked with 300 μL of electrolyte, and the coated graphite paper samples were placed in vacuum-sealed bags (Figure S17).

Galvanostatic charge/discharge tests were conducted on the full cell using BTS4000 power equipment at various current densities, with the voltage range set between 0.1 and 2.0 V. The specific capacitance of the symmetric cell (C cell, F/g) was calculated using the following formula 3 Ccell=(I)(Δt)m(ΔV)

The specific capacitance of the electrode (C electrode, F/g) in the two-electrode system, based on galvanostatic charge–discharge measurements, was calculated using the following formula 4 Celectrode=4(I)(Δt)m(ΔV)

The specific power density (P s, W/kg) and energy density (E s, Wh/kg) of the fabricated cell were determined using the relationships provided below 5 Ps=IΔVm(10−3)
6 Es=PsΔt3600 where Δt is the discharging time (s), m is the total mass of materials in both electrodes (g), I is the applied current (A), and ΔV is the voltage window (V).

sec.title: Morphology of the As-Synthesized SE_GLC
sec.p: The morphology of SE_GLC was examined using SEM, which revealed a 3D interconnected network structure (Figure A,B). Further characterization using TEM (Figure C,D) demonstrated the congregation of graphene-like structures with a slightly wrinkled surface, indicative of few-layered graphene-like morphologies. ,, The observed wrinkles in SE_GLC materials facilitate ion diffusion and reduce the charge transfer resistance. This unique feature, distinct from the morphologies of pristine Sesbania and SE_HTC (Figure S1), is primarily attributed to the hydrothermal carbonization and KOH activation processes. Sesbania was chosen as the precursor due to its cost-effectiveness, renewability, and a layered structure composed of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin (Figure S2). During hydrothermal carbonization, nitric acid (HNO3) assists in exfoliating the biomass into a layered structure. The bulky cellulose in Sesbania is broken down and partially hydrolyzed by the addition of the acid. , Furthermore, nitric acid promotes dehydration in the biomass, further facilitating the hydrothermal carbonization process. Post-HTC processing results in the carbonization of most hemicellulose and lignin, along with partial decomposition of cellulose. , During KOH activation, K ions intercalate into the material layers, playing a pivotal role in forming the interconnected porous graphene-like structure. ,, After hydrothermal carbonization removes the outer layer of Sesbania (compose of hemicellulose and lignin), potassium ions intercalate into the inner cellulose layer, loosening its structure. This layer is then graphitized and transformed into an interconnected graphene-like structure during high-temperature activation. The resulting 3D porous network prevents restacking and agglomeration of graphene-like sheets while enhancing electrochemical performance by facilitating electron transfer and shortening ion transport pathways. ,, Further insights into the elemental composition of Sesbania, SE_HTC and SE_GLC are provided in Figure S2–S4.

caption.p: (A, B) SEM images and (C, D) TEM images of SE_GLC.

sec.title: Structures of the As-Synthesized SE_GLC
sec.p:
The graphitic characteristics of SE_HTC and SE_GLC were examined using Raman spectroscopy. The Raman spectrum of SE_HTC (Figure S5) showed the D peak at 1359 cm–1 and the G peak at 1585 cm–1, with a broad region between these two peaks indicating the presence of amorphous carbon in SE_HTC. The G peak corresponds to sp2-hybridized carbon atoms, while the D peak signifies carbon lattice defects. ,, Nevertheless, the Raman spectrum of SE_GLC displayed three distinct peaks: the D peak at 1342 cm–1, the G peak at 1574 cm–1, and the 2D peak at 2688 cm–1 (Figure A). The sharp 2D peak without a shoulder and the I 2D/I G ratio (0.47) confirm the presence of multilayered graphene in the SE_GLC structure. ,−
Additionally, the low I D/I G ratio (0.59) indicates a high degree of graphitization with minimal multilayer structural defects. These results suggest that SE_GLC has a porous graphene-like structure. Figure B shows the N2 adsorption–desorption isotherms of the SE_GLC material. The typical type I and IV isotherms suggest the presence of both micro- and mesopores in the material. The H4-type hysteresis loop in the isotherm indicates a micromesoporous structure with slit-shaped pores. , The pore size distribution (Figure C) further confirms numerous micropores in SE_GLC. Furthermore, SE_GLC exhibited a large specific surface area of 1140 m2/g and an average pore diameter of 2.18 nm (Table S1). This porous graphene-like structure is expected to promote mass transport, thereby improving the power density of supercapacitors. The gas adsorption–desorption isotherm and pore size distribution of the SE_HTC material are also shown in Figure S6. The low specific surface area and small pore volume of SE_HTC (Table S1) highlight the importance of chemical activation in enhancing the porosity of SE_GLC. The structure of the as-prepared materials was also studied by using X-ray diffraction (XRD). The SE_GLC exhibited large diffraction peaks at approximately 26.5, 42.9, 44, 49, and 54°, corresponding to the (002), (020), (111), (022), and (004) planes of graphite (JCPDS 41–1487), respectively (Figure D). The XRD pattern also revealed characteristic peaks of graphite and Fe3C (ICDD 01–072–1110) (Figure S7). As a leguminous plant, Sesbania relies on iron for nitrogen fixation, absorbing it from soil and water, transporting it via the xylem to root nodules, and storing it in the stem and cellulose structure. During the high-temperature synthesis process, the cellulose structure is broken down, releasing the iron it contains. A portion of this iron is not completely removed during synthesis and reacts with carbon to form Fe3C. However, the presence of Fe3C could promote the formation of a graphene-like structure in the carbon materials. , The microporous nature of the material was further shown by high-intensity diffraction peaks at small angles. The calculated d 002 interlayer distance was 0.336 nm, indicating that the synthesized carbon material, graphene-like, possesses an interlayer distance consistent with graphene and distinct from the more compact structure of graphite. , Additionally, the XRD pattern of SE_HTC is shown in Figure S8. WAXS profiles of the obtained carbon materials, as presented in Figure S9, displayed characteristic peaks consistent with the XRD results. The WAXS profiles of SE_HTC also confirm the partial decomposition of cellulose during hydrothermal carbonization. The chemical structure of SE_HTC and SE_GLC was further analyzed using FTIR spectroscopy (Figure S10). Both FTIR spectra of SE_HTC and SE_GLC exhibited a peak at 1642 cm–1, attributed to the CC vibration, ,, along with peaks at approximately 3285, 1241, 1151, and 1020 cm–1 corresponding to the stretching vibrations of O–H, C–OH, C–O–C, and C–O functional groups, respectively. ,,,, Interestingly, SE_HTC exhibited additional peaks at 2910 and 2850 cm–1, assigned to the asymmetric and symmetric stretching vibrations of C–H hydroxyl groups, respectively. In contrast, the peak at 2850 cm–1 was absent in SE_GLC, suggesting degradation of the structural constituents of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin during the high-temperature chemical activation. ,, XPS analysis was also employed to investigate the surface chemistry, chemical composition, and functional groups of SE_GLC. Based on the wide-scan survey (Figure S11A), SE_GLC primarily consisted of C 1s (85.9 atom %), O 1s (9.2 atom %), and N 1s (3.9 atom %). Minor contributions from Si 2p (0.08 atom %) and Fe 2p (0.02 atom %) were also detected. The deconvolution of the high-resolution C 1s spectrum provided detailed insights into the chemical bonding environment of SE_GLC (Figure S11B), ,, and the surface functionalities identified from the C 1s spectra are summarized in Table S2. In addition, the deconvoluted high-resolution O 1s spectrum (Figure S8C) and N 1s spectrum (Figure S11D) were analyzed, with the corresponding functional groups also listed in Table S2. ,−
These oxygen-containing functional groups are expected to enhance the surface energy and wettability of SE_GLC with aqueous electrolytes, improving ion accessibility and facilitating charge transfer processes. Consequently, these properties contribute to the high electrochemical performance of the SE_GLC electrode.

caption.p: (A) Raman spectrum, (B) N2 adsorption–desorption isotherms, (C) pore size distribution, and (D) XRD pattern of SE_GLC.

sec.title: Electrochemical Performance of the As-Prepared Materials
sec.p: The electrochemical properties of the as-prepared materials were first tested using a three-electrode system in 1 m NaNO3 aqueous electrolyte. Figure A depicts the quasi-rectangular CV curves without peaks for both the SE_HTC and SE_GLC electrodes, suggesting electrical double-layer capacitive behavior. The calculated specific capacitance of the SE_GLC was 43 F/g, which surpassed that of the SE_HTC electrode (29 F/g). In addition, the CV curves of the SE_GLC electrode without significant distortion could be observed when increasing the scan rate, indicating the rapid ion transport compared to the SE_HTC electrode (Figure S12). The Nyquist plot of the SE_GLC electrode, along with the fitted equivalent circuit (Figure S13A and Table S3), further demonstrated a lower equivalent series resistance (ESR) compared to the SE_HTC electrode. In the low-frequency range, the oblique line of the SE_GLC curve was also closest to the vertical axis, indicating capacitive characteristics and fast ion transport. These findings suggest that the enhanced electrochemical performance of SE_GLC can be attributed to its 3D interconnected graphene-like structure, which facilitates ion adsorption and diffusion. Further testing of SE_GLC electrodes was conducted in a water-in-salt NaNO3 electrolyte. It was observed that increasing the concentration of NaNO3 salt in the electrolyte resulted in higher viscosity, a trend consistent across highly concentrated electrolytes (Figure S14). Notably, the highest ionic conductivity of 180.50 mS/cm at room temperature was achieved at a concentration of 12 m NaNO3, surpassing that of commonly used highly concentrated electrolytes, such as 17 m NaClO4. As shown in Figure B, the operating potential window expanded with increasing salt concentration, reaching 1.9 V in 12 m NaNO3. This expansion indicates suppressed water splitting, attributed to the limited availability of free water molecules in the WIS electrolyte. In the 12 m NaNO3 electrolyte, Na+ ions are primarily solvated by water molecules. The CV curves of the SE_GLC electrode in 12 m NaNO3 electrolyte (Figure C) retained their quasi-rectangular shape across various scan rates, demonstrating good rate capability and low resistance of the WIS electrolyte. At scan rates of 10, 20, 50, and 100 mV/s, the specific capacitances of the SE_GLC electrode in 12 m NaNO3 were 250, 101, 51, and 43 F/g, respectively (Figure D). The galvanostatic charge–discharge measurements of SE_GLC in 12 m NaNO3 were conducted at various current densities from 0.1 to 2 A/g (Figure S15). The resulting GCD curves exhibited a quasi-triangular shape, indicative of capacitive behavior consistent with the CV findings. The specific capacitances determined at 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1, and 2 A/g were approximately 187, 146, 122, 112, 102, and 89 F/g, respectively. For comparison, the specific capacitances in 1 m, 3 m, and 7 m NaNO3 were 116, 28, 12, and 6 F/g; 199, 61, 33, and 7 F/g; and 204, 65, 38, and 15 F/g, respectively. The increase in specific capacitance of the carbon-based electrode with the WIS electrolyte (12 m NaNO3) aligns with previously reported studies. ,,, This improvement in electrochemical performance is attributed to changes in hydrated ionic solvation shells and the enhanced conductivity of the WIS electrolyte. ,, Supplementary EIS results confirmed the low ESR of the SE_GLC electrode in the highly concentrated electrolyte (12 m NaNO3) compared to other NaNO3 concentrations (Figure S13B and Table S3).

caption.p: (A) CV of SE_HTC and SE_GLC electrodes in 1 m NaNO3 electrolyte, (B) CV of the SE_GLC electrode in 1 m, 3 m, 7 m, and 12 m NaNO3 electrolytes, (C) CV curves at various potential scan rates (10–100 mV/s) of the SE_GLC electrode in 12 m NaNO3 electrolyte, and (D) Specific capacitances of the SE_GLC electrode in 1 m, 3 m, 7 m, and 12 m NaNO3 electrolytes. These tests were conducted using a three-electrode setup.

sec.p: To further analyze the relative contributions of capacitive and diffusion-controlled processes to the charge storage behavior of the SE_GLC electrode, we applied a power-law relationship between scan rate (v) and current (i), expressed as log­(i) = log­(a) + b·log­(v). A b-value close to 1 suggests capacitive behavior (e.g., electric double-layer capacitance), whereas a b-value near 0.5 indicates diffusion-limited intercalation processes. , As shown in Figure S16, the SE_GLC electrode exhibited b-values close to 1 for a charge process, confirming that charge storage is dominated by capacitive mechanisms with rapid kinetics. This conclusion is further supported by Dunn’s method, which separates current response into capacitive and diffusion-controlled contributions using the relation i(V) = k 1 v + k 2 v 1/2, where k 1 and k 2 represent capacitive and diffusion-controlled processes, respectively. ,,, The red region in Figure A highlighted the capacitive contribution at a scan rate of 10 mV/s. A bar chart summarizing the capacitance contribution across scan rates from 10 to 100 mV/s is also included (Figure B). At 10 mV/s, the SE_GLC electrode exhibited a capacitive contribution as high as 94.81%, clearly indicating that electric double-layer capacitance is the dominant charge storage mechanism. In contrast, the pseudocapacitive contribution, attributable to redox-active oxygen-containing functional groups and possible Fe3C impurities, was limited to approximately 5.19%. Moreover, as the scan rate increased, the capacitive contribution further rose, which can be attributed to the highly porous structure of SE_GLC that supports rapid ion transport. The oxygen-containing functional groups also help improve surface wettability and ion accessibility, supporting rapid, capacitive charge storage.

caption.p: (A) Capacitance contribution of SE_GLC in 12 m NaNO3, showing capacitive behavior (red region) and diffusion-controlled behavior (gray region) at 10 mV/s; and (B) histograms of the capacitance contribution of SE_GLC in 12 m NaNO3 at different scan rates (10–100 mV/s).

sec.p: To evaluate practical applications, symmetric full cells based on two SE_GLC electrodes were fabricated using 12 m NaNO3 as the electrolyte (Figure S17). The stability window of the fabricated pouch cell was investigated by varying the voltage window during CV measurements. It was found that the stability voltage of the SE_GLC//SE_GLC cell reached 1.9 V with the WIS electrolyte (Figure A). This result confirms the broader voltage window of the WIS electrolyte compared to the salt-in-water electrolyte. In addition, the CV curves exhibited a typical rectangular shape, indicating that the dominant electrochemical reaction is EDLC. At a scan rate of 100 mV/s, the CV curves maintained a symmetrical quasi-rectangular shape, indicating rapid ion transfer within the interconnected graphene-like structure of the electrode (Figure B). As shown in Figure C, galvanostatic charge–discharge profiles were obtained at various current densities, ranging from 0.1 to 3 A/g. The GCD profiles for the SE_GLC//SE_GLC pouch cell show a quasi-triangular shape, suggesting capacitive behavior consistent with the CV results. The specific capacitances of the SE_GLC//SE_GLC cell were found to be 24, 17, 15, 13, and 10 F/g at current densities of 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, and 3 A/g, respectively (Figure D). The specific capacitance of the SE_GLC electrode was calculated to be 96 F/g at 0.1 A/g. The slight performance drops of SE_GLC at high current densities are attributed to its 3D interconnected graphene-like structure, featuring both mesopores and micropores that facilitate efficient ion adsorption and diffusion. Nevertheless, operating near the salt solubility limit introduces additional constraints in water-in-salt electrolytes. Water hydrolysis at high voltages may result in partial water loss and subsequent salt crystallization. These crystallized salts can obstruct the porous network, further impeding ion transport and reducing the overall capacitance of the cell. The highest gravimetric energy density of the SE_GLC//SE_GLC cell in 12 m NaNO3 electrolyte was 23.83 Wh/kg at a specific power density of 189.83 W/kg, achieved at a current density of 0.1 A/g. Even at a high power density of 5.69 kW/kg, the energy density was maintained at approximately 9.49 Wh/kg. The cycling stability of the SE_GLC//SE_GLC cell is shown in Figure F. The fabricated pouch cell retained 84.05% of its initial capacitance after 1000 cycles. In contrast, when 1 m NaNO3 was used as the electrolyte, the fabricated cell exhibited a specific capacitance of approximately 10 F/g at 0.1 A/g, with the cycling stability dropping to approximately 72.58% (Figure S18). Additional details on the electrochemical performance of the SE_GLC//SE_GLC cell in 1 m and 12 m NaNO3 are presented in Figure S19 and Table S4. However, previous research has indicated that water-in-salt electrolytes present unique challenges compared to traditional salt-in-water aqueous electrolytes. These challenges include corrosion of current collectors at high salt concentrations, increased water electrolysis, and higher viscosity or cell resistance at elevated operating voltages. , Furthermore, the performance of the SE_GLC//SE_GLC cell with 12 m NaNO3 is comparable to other graphene-like-based aqueous supercapacitors (Table S5). The use of the WIS electrolyte also enabled a wider operating voltage than previously reported for graphene-like aqueous supercapacitors. Therefore, the superior electrochemical performance of the SE_GLC//SE_GLC supercapacitor is attributed to the interconnected graphene-like structure of the SE_GLC electrode, which provides a large surface area. While the presence of Fe3C may have a minor influence, its primary role is to facilitate the formation of the graphene-like structure rather than directly contributing to charge storage. The 3D porous network of SE_GLC also prevents restacking of carbon nanosheets, facilitates rapid charge and electrolyte diffusion, and provides efficient channels for charge storage. The implementation of the WIS electrolyte also widened the voltage window, thereby enhancing both the power and energy densities of the symmetric supercapacitors. Finally, the NaNO3 WIS electrolyte is cost-effective compared to other WIS-based electrolytes, which makes it a promising candidate for further development of aqueous WIS-based supercapacitors.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The successful synthesis of graphene-like porous material from Sesbania, an abundant biomass waste, through a simple acid-assisted hydrothermal carbonization process followed by chemical activation, represents a significant advancement in the development of sustainable graphene-like materials. The SE_GLC material features a unique 3D interconnected porous structure within graphene-like layers, achieving a specific surface area of up to 1140 m2/g. This structure facilitates efficient ion and charge storage and diffusion. Using a cost-effective NaNO3 WIS electrolyte, the SE_GLC material was incorporated into a symmetric aqueous supercapacitor, achieving an expanded operating voltage of 1.9 V. Notably, the SE_GLC//SE_GLC pouch cell attained a maximum gravimetric energy density of 23.83 Wh/kg at a gravimetric power density of 189.83 W/kg. Even at a high specific power density of 5.69 kW/kg, the specific energy density remained stable at approximately 9.49 Wh/kg. Additionally, the SE_GLC//SE_GLC cell, utilizing the 12 m NaNO3 electrolyte, demonstrated excellent capacitance retention of 84.05% after 1000 cycles. This study provides a solid foundation for the further exploration of cost-effective WIS-related energy storage systems and the development of graphene-like porous materials from biomass sources.
